title: Asymmetry: session-mix latency & cost vignette
content:
Executive summary:

This vignette explores how asymmetric session mixes (many short-turn sessions + a small proportion of long-context, streaming sessions) change the combined latency/cost surface. Goal is an operational checklist for routing and batching knobs that yield the best price-performance for typical PLG applications. This is a lightweight, reproducible writeup with compact ASCII charts and suggested follow-ups.

Key takeaways (quick):
- Short-chat dominant traffic (80% of sessions < 3 turns) makes aggressive batching + prefix caching attractive: p95 latency can be kept < 120ms while cutting per-token cost by ~18% vs no batching.
- Long-context sessions (top 5% by length) dominate token volume and cost: targeted routing to quantized variants reduces total spend by up to 22% with <5% p99 latency regression for short sessions.
- Streaming sessions (interleaved) create tail spikes; a small dedicated pool with relaxed batching windows stabilizes p99 at acceptable cost.

Workload definitions used here:
- short-chat: median 2 turns, median 40 tokens per response, session duration < 30s.
- medium-dialog: 6-12 turns, responses 60-150 tokens, typical duration 1-3 minutes.
- long-context: 1-3 sessions/day, responses 400-2,000 tokens, often single-shot summarization or chain-of-thought.
- streaming sessions: chunked token emission, low initial latency requirement, high sustained token rate.

Bench setup (brief):
- Models: rwd-13B-fp16 (baseline), rwd-13B-int4 (quantized), rwd-70B-fp16 (large), rwd-6B-fp16 (small).
- Hardware: A100-80GB (core pool), A10G (edge pool), isolated small pool: T4.
- Batching knobs tested: windowed batching (3–50ms), cadence-based session grouping (1–8 concurrent turns), KV prefix cache with TTL 10s/60s.
- Workload generator: synthetic mix derived from production event-sample (made deterministic).
- Metrics collected: p50/p90/p95/p99 latency per response, tokens-per-second per GPU, cost estimate = cloud GPU cost prorated + per-model license (normalized cost units).

Representative results table (aggregated across 2h runs):

Scenario | session mix | batching | cache | p95 (ms) | p99 (ms) | tokens/GPU/hr | relative cost
---------|--------------|---------|-------|----------|---------|---------------|--------------
A | 80/15/5 (S/M/L) | off | none | 450 | 980 | 80k | 1.00
B | 80/15/5 | window 20ms | TTL10s | 170 | 380 | 120k | 0.82
C | 80/15/5 | window 20ms + cadence | TTL60s | 140 | 290 | 140k | 0.75
D | 75/10/15 | window 20ms + cadence | TTL60s + routed quant | 160 | 360 | 125k | 0.78
E | 80/15/5 + 3% streaming | window 10ms | TTL10s + dedicated stream pool | 180 | 240 | 110k | 0.86

Notes on table: relative cost normalized to Scenario A baseline. Scenario C represents sweet spot for our synthetic PLG mix.

ASCII visual: p95 comparison (lower is better)

Scenario A: █████████████████████████▉ 450ms
Scenario B: ████████████▍ 170ms
Scenario C: ██████████ 140ms
Scenario D: ███████████ 160ms
Scenario E: ███████████▋ 180ms

Token volume skew (long-context heavy): top-5% sessions = 62% of tokens. Implication: optimizations must be token-aware, not session-count-aware.

Observations (detailed):
1) Batching windows: 15–25ms windows yield most of the throughput wins for short sessions without measurably hurting p50 latency. Beyond 30ms diminishing returns and poor UX for interactive clients.
2) KV prefix cache: TTL 10s improves short-session p95 by ~40% in our synthetic trace; TTL 60s yields additional throughput but increases staleness risk for dynamic content. Recommend TTL tiering by route.
3) Quantized variants: routing long-context jobs to int4 variants reduces GPU-hours by 18–28% depending on model, but requires careful fallbacks; for mixed sessions, automated fallback after a mild quality regression detection (A/B prompt tests) is necessary.
4) Streaming: mixing streaming with window batching creates tail amplification. A small dedicated stream pool with looser batching (10ms) and higher concurrency prevents p99 spikes for short sessions.
5) Cost accounting: using tokens/GPU/hr as proxy correlates but misses pre-warm and cold-start overheads — for low-throughput customers, reserved capacity assumptions change recommendations.

Recommendations (ops + product):
- Routing: implement session classifier to send sessions > 400 tokens to quantized variants or dedicated long-context pools. Flagging threshold configurable per-customer. (JIRA-ENG-4123)
- Batching defaults: set window to 20ms for hosted default; allow per-route override. Expose recommended guardrails in Console.
- Caching policy: TTL tiers (10s for chat, 60s for assistant memory retrieval) exposed as hints; enable adaptive TTL that extends for repeated prefixes.
- Streaming pool: deploy a small dedicated stream pool with autoscale down to 1 GPU. Use lower-precision variant for sustained throughput.
- Monitoring: add a composite metric (tokens-weighted p95) to prioritize regressions driven by token-heavy sessions.

Open questions / follow-ups:
- Quality impact matrix for int4 on chain-of-thought tasks: need 50-case evals across common prompt families. (Assigned: Arjun)
- How do cold start amortization effects change for customers on reserved Dedicated pools? Need to run week-long simulations.
- Can we instrument prefix similarity on real traffic to tune cache TTL adaptively without leaking PII?

Appendix: small reproducible config snippets (pseudo):
- session-classifier: if estimated_total_tokens > 400 -> route: long-context-pool
- batching: window_ms: 20, max_batch_tokens: 8192
- cache: enabled: true, tiers: [{route_hint: chat, ttl: 10}, {route_hint: long-context, ttl: 60}]

Repro notes / artifacts:
- synthetic trace snapshot: s3://benchmarks/sep03-2025/session-mix-v1 (internal)
- runtime PR: https://github.com/redwood-inference/runtime/pull/987 (batching window expose)
- Ticket for routing policy: JIRA-ENG-4123

Action items (next 2 weeks):
- Prototype session classifier + routing in staging (owner: Maya)
- Small eval of int4 quality on 5 prompt families (owner: Arjun)
- Console UX draft to expose batching TTLs and routing hints (owner: Zoe)

Raw notes (in-progress):
- saw one odd outlier where p99 jumped to 2.2s during run C for a brief 6m window; trace points to a GC spike in runtime process on one node. Need SRE input.
- we should consider cost modeling that includes prewarm amortization for low-QPS customers; current relative cost numbers assume steady-state sustained-run pricing.

If useful I can paste the full CSV export, flamegraphs, and the synthetic trace. This is intentionally short — thinking notes for product/ops sync.

-- Maya
